questions.q: A log file has 50,000 lines. Why would you reach for `less` instead of `cat` to read it?
options: cat cannot open files larger than 1,000 lines
less lets you page through the file and search it, without flooding your terminal with the entire contents at once
less is required for any file ending in .log
cat and less produce different file contents
questions.explain: cat prints the whole file immediately, which scrolls past before you can read it for long files. less loads the file for paged, searchable viewing one screen at a time.

questions.q: You want to watch a deploy log update live while a deployment is running. Which command do you use?
options: head -f deploy.log
cat deploy.log
tail -f deploy.log
grep -f deploy.log
questions.explain: tail -f ('follow') keeps the file open and prints new lines as they're appended, which is exactly what's needed to watch a log in real time. It runs until stopped with Ctrl+C.

options: Deletes every line containing the word 'error'
Counts how many lines contain the word 'error'
Searches deploy.log case-insensitively for 'error' and prints each matching line with its line number
Replaces 'error' with 'ERROR' throughout the file
questions.explain: -i makes the search case-insensitive and -n prefixes each matching line with its line number. grep never modifies the file — it only prints matching lines.

questions.q: By default, how many lines do `head` and `tail` each show?
options: All lines in the file
The first and last 10 lines, respectively
Only 1 line each
head shows 10 lines, but tail shows the entire file
questions.explain: Both head and tail default to showing 10 lines — head from the start of the file, tail from the end. The -n flag changes that count on either command.

options: The file's size in bytes
The number of words in the file
The number of lines in the file
The number of lowercase letters in the file
questions.explain: wc normally reports lines, words, and bytes together. The -l flag narrows that down to just the line count, which is a quick way to size up a file before deciding how to read it.
